lead: A radar sends out a burst of radio energy and listens for the echo. The round-trip delay of the echo gives the range of the target, and the direction the antenna points gives its bearing. Every other part of a radar exists to make those two measurements reliably in noise and clutter. The same idea runs air traffic control at an airport, weather radar over the Bay of Bengal, a police speed gun on the highway and the radio altimeter of an aircraft. This chapter builds the pulse radar block diagram and then chooses a frequency band for the job.
prereq: You need antenna gain and beamwidth from Antenna fundamentals and radiation, and the speed of light, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

sections.h3: Delay gives range, pointing gives direction

blocks.text: Radar is short for radio detection and ranging. The transmitter sends a short pulse, the antenna focuses it into a beam, and any target in the beam reflects a tiny part of it back. The receiver notes when the echo arrives.

blocks.where: R is the target range in metres; c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light; t is the round-trip delay of the echo in seconds.

blocks.text: The 2 is there because the wave goes out and comes back, so only half of the delay belongs to the outward trip. A handy rule: every 1 µs of delay is 150 m of range, so 124 µs is 18.6 km.

Direction comes from the antenna. A narrow beam gives a precise bearing in azimuth and elevation, so the beamwidth sets the angle accuracy. A moving target also shifts the echo frequency; that Doppler shift gives speed and is the subject of CW and FMCW radar.
A pulse of width τ occupies cτ metres of space. Two targets on the same bearing are seen as two only if their echoes do not overlap, which needs a range difference of at least half the pulse length:

blocks.where: ΔR is the range resolution in metres; τ is the pulse width in seconds.

blocks.text: A monostatic radar uses one antenna for transmit and receive, which is the usual case and the one this unit assumes. A bistatic radar has its transmitter and receiver at separate sites.
The figure shows the blocks and the path of the pulse and the echo. Each block has one job:

items: Synchronizer (timer): the master clock. It sets the pulse repetition frequency (PRF), triggers the modulator, and starts the range count at the instant the pulse leaves.

Modulator: in a radar built around a magnetron or klystron, it is the high-voltage pulse generator that switches the transmitter tube on for exactly τ seconds. In a solid-state radar a low-power generator forms the pulse and the amplifiers raise it.
Transmitter: produces the high-power pulse, from kilowatts to megawatts peak with a magnetron, klystron, TWT or solid-state amplifiers.
Duplexer: a switch that connects the antenna to the transmitter during the pulse and to the receiver between pulses. It uses TR and ATR gas tubes or a ferrite circulator with a limiter.
Antenna: a high-gain reflector or array that forms the beam and scans it, mechanically or electronically.
Receiver: a superheterodyne chain (low-noise amplifier, mixer, IF amplifier, detector); the echo reaches it only through the duplexer.
Signal processor: matched filtering, clutter rejection (MTI or pulse Doppler) and the detection threshold.
Display: a plan position indicator (PPI) shows each target at its range and bearing.

blocks.text: Radar bands carry letter names (the IEEE letter bands). The edges are conventions, and other standards draw them slightly differently.

head: Band
Frequency
Typical use
rows: very long range surveillance, foliage penetration
weather radar, aircraft radio altimeters (4.2–4.4 GHz)
marine radar, airborne radar, speed guns (10.525 GHz)
speed guns (24.15 GHz); water vapour absorbs near 22 GHz

blocks.text: Choose the band by the job, not by a ranking. Lower bands lose less to the air and to rain, and they see less rain clutter, because rain backscatter rises steeply with frequency. Their cost is size: beamwidth grows with wavelength, so a narrow low-band beam needs a big antenna, and the wider beam lights up a larger patch of ground. Higher bands give a narrow beam from a small antenna and support short pulses for fine resolution, but rain attenuation rises and high transmitter power is harder to build.

So long-range air surveillance sits at L band, airport and weather radar at S band, airborne radar at X band, and car radar at 77 GHz, where a hand-sized antenna still gives a narrow beam. Refraction, ducting and rain loss are covered in Antenna arrays, types and propagation.

examples.question: A pulse radar transmits a 1 µs pulse. The echo from a target arrives 124 µs after the pulse leaves the antenna. Find (a) the target range, (b) the length of the pulse in space and (c) the range resolution.
steps: Pulse length in space: c τ = 3 × 10⁸ × 1 × 10⁻⁶ = 300 m.
Range resolution: ΔR = c τ / 2 = 300 / 2 = 150 m.
Check with the rule of thumb: 124 µs × 150 m per µs = 18 600 m.
examples.answer: R = 18.6 km; the pulse is 300 m long in space; two targets on the same bearing must be at least 150 m apart in range to be seen as two.

examples.question: An air surveillance radar needs a 1.5° beamwidth. Using θ ≈ 70λ/D degrees for a dish of diameter D, find the dish size at L band (1.3 GHz), S band (2.8 GHz) and X band (9.4 GHz), and say which band a rooftop installation would choose.
steps: Rearrange: D = 70λ/θ, with θ in degrees and λ = c/f.
The same beam needs a dish about 7 times larger at L band than at X band, because D grows in proportion to λ.
examples.answer: D ≈ 10.8 m at L band, 5.0 m at S band and 1.49 m at X band. A rooftop set would take X band for its small antenna, accepting more rain loss; a long-range airport radar accepts the larger S-band antenna to keep rain loss low.

traps: Writing R = c t instead of R = c t / 2. The delay covers the trip out and back.
Mixing up the pulse length in space, cτ, with the range resolution, cτ/2. The resolution is half the pulse length.
Drawing the antenna straight into the receiver. On receive the echo passes back through the duplexer; on transmit the duplexer cuts the receiver off.
Treating band letters as exact limits, or assuming a higher band is always better. Rain loss and transmitter power can make a high band worse for long range.

quiz.q: What does radar stand for, and which two quantities does a basic pulse radar measure?
quiz.a: Radio detection and ranging. It measures range from the echo delay and direction from the antenna pointing angle.

quiz.q: State the function of the synchronizer and of the modulator in a pulse radar.
quiz.a: The synchronizer is the master timer: it sets the PRF, triggers the modulator and starts the range count. The modulator is the high-voltage pulse generator that switches the transmitter tube on for the pulse width τ.

quiz.q: Why does the range equation R = c t / 2 contain a factor 2?
quiz.a: The wave travels from the antenna to the target and back. The measured delay t covers both trips, so the one-way distance is half of c t.

quiz.q: A radar transmits a 0.5 µs pulse and the echo arrives 60 µs later. Find the range and the range resolution.
State the job of the duplexer and name the two gas tubes used in a classic duplexer.
quiz.a: It lets one antenna serve the transmitter and the receiver: during the pulse it connects the transmitter to the antenna and shields the receiver; between pulses it connects the antenna to the receiver. The tubes are the TR (transmit-receive) and ATR (anti-transmit-receive) tubes.

quiz.q: An L-band radar at 1.5 GHz and an X-band radar at 10 GHz have dishes of the same diameter. Which has the narrower beam, and by how much? Use θ ≈ 70λ/D.
quiz.a: λ is 0.2 m at 1.5 GHz and 0.03 m at 10 GHz. With the same D, θ is proportional to λ, so the X-band beam is narrower by 0.2/0.03 = 6.7 times.

quiz.q: Why does a weather radar meant to measure heavy rain at 200 km use S band rather than X band?
quiz.a: Rain attenuation grows steeply with frequency. At X band a heavy storm near the radar would absorb much of the beam, so storms behind it would look weaker or vanish. S band passes through heavy rain with little loss; the price is a larger antenna for the same beamwidth.

beyond: Most new radars are active electronically scanned arrays (AESA), with a small solid-state transmit/receive module behind each element, so the beam moves in microseconds with no moving parts. Car radar at 76–81 GHz, ground-penetrating radar for road surveys and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging from satellites are fast-growing areas. Search for AESA, automotive FMCW radar and SAR imaging to go further.

spec.aria: Block diagram. Top row: synchronizer, modulator, transmitter, duplexer, then a dish antenna. The echo returns from the antenna to the duplexer and down to the receiver, then left to the signal processor and the display. A dashed line from the synchronizer to the display marks range zero. Below, a time axis from 0 to 150 microseconds shows the 1 microsecond pulse at zero and the echo at 124 microseconds, giving 18.6 km.
